prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction and experimental discovery of time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect

statement.case_for: I keep B018 as my single preferred part and my position has not changed since round 1. Kane and Mele showed that spin-orbit coupling in graphene yields a Z2-classified time-reversal-invariant insulator with protected helical edge states, and Molenkamp's group observed the corresponding edge-channel conduction in HgTe/CdTe wells. This is a symmetry-based organising principle, not a method or an instrument: it defines a new class of band insulators, with stable interpretation, reproduction in 2D and 3D materials by transport and photoemission over about two decades, and no open question about what was observed. The round-1 exchange showed that B018 is the common first alternative of the B041 camp as well, so it is the configuration least likely to be judged wrong by any member's own criteria. For the chair's question on criteria, I would let two things decide between B018 and B041: whether the discovery is a new state of matter or a new measurement regime, and whether the interpretation is settled. On both, B018 is the stronger claim now, although I regard B041 as a prize-worthy result.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the central weakness. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal guided the experiment, and the 3D work of Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hasan and others sits at the edge of the citation, so three names tell an incomplete history; Zhang's death does not remove the fairness question. I have not wanted to hide this. My answer to the chair is that it is tolerable only if the citation is narrowed to the time-reversal-invariant topological insulator and the quantum spin Hall effect, and if the committee records in deliberation that the BHZ proposal identified where to look but did not originate the Z2 concept or its first realistic material proposal, and that the 3D programme is a separate, later achievement that is not being judged. The 2016 overlap is a second concern, which I judge weaker: that prize concerned quantisation and phase transitions in quantum Hall and chain systems, while Z2 insulators protected by time reversal are a different symmetry class. A final point against: my own opening ranked B030 first, so I may be overcorrecting toward settled interpretation.

responses.point: Kroll and Lindroth argue that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct mechanism from the 2005 comb and 2012 individual-quantum-system prizes, and that the claim is clean with two names and no exclusions.
responses.response: I accept that distinction as real and I think a citation around neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice can be written. What I do not accept is that a clean attribution decides the matter. Cleanness is a virtue, but a prize for an instrument whose accuracy regime is the achievement is a different kind of discovery from a new class of matter, and in precision metrology the redefinition of the second is still prospective. I also note that I am not the best judge of priority details in precision spectroscopy. If the committee goes to B041 I would not object on scientific grounds, and I rank it as my first alternative; I would only ask that the citation be anchored on the lattice and magic wavelength, as Kroll proposes.

responses.point: Johansson says that if a citation separating B041 from the 2005 and 2012 prizes cannot be written convincingly, B018 is the safer choice and he lists it first among his alternatives.
responses.response: This is the most useful statement in the round for the choice between our camps, because it shows that the disagreement is about citation wording and not about quality. If Johansson, Kroll and Lindroth would accept B018 with the narrowed citation, and I would accept B041 with the lattice-anchored citation, the committee is choosing on a criterion and not on a quarrel about evidence. I think the stronger criterion is new phase of matter against new measurement regime, and the stronger side of it is B018. I would add that B041 faces an unresolved timing question (redefinition of the second), while B018 faces an attribution question that no further waiting will resolve. That asymmetry favours acting on B018 now.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the 3D topological-insulator work of Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Hasan is a large share of the field's impact, so a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize rests on a framing choice that colleagues will contest.
responses.response: I agree it is a framing choice and I think it should be made openly. The honest framing is a prize for the quantum spin Hall effect, a predicted phase and its experimental observation, not for topological insulators as a field. Under that framing Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents, and Hasan's ARPES results are a distinct 3D achievement, and one of them (Kane) is already inside the trio for the 2D work. The 3D programme could be recognised separately later, though I admit that three names make it difficult to honour both. This does not remove your concern; it states precisely what the prize would and would not claim.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B030 as a second alternative and says he would not object to it as lead if timing were weighed differently, while keeping B018 first because its interpretation is stable.
responses.response: I agree with the reasoning and with the symmetry in our positions: we both regard B030 as strong, and both defer it because the origin of the correlated and superconducting phases is open and the main experiments date from 2018. I would not argue that B030 is wrong; I think it will be a stronger candidate with a longer record. I remain willing to see it as lead only if the committee judges that the reproduced observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity is enough without a settled mechanism, which my own earlier ranking assumed and which colleagues, especially Eriksson and Olsson, have persuaded me is too optimistic for this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts omitting Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the 3D contributors under a narrowed quantum spin Hall citation, and what the deliberation record should say about it.
Whether the 2016 prize on topological phases is judged to leave enough room for time-reversal-invariant insulators as a separate discovery.
Whether new phase of matter against new measurement regime is the right criterion between B018 and B041, or whether the pending redefinition of the second should count for B041.
Whether the open mechanism of the correlated phases in twisted bilayer graphene should still keep B030 back, or whether it should be held for a later year.
My knowledge of detailed priority sequences is from memory and has not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: No change. I have no documented connection to any credited name on the shortlist: my listed co-authors and institutions (Fulde, Gustavsson, Wilkinson, Einarsson, Candelier, Pumir, Meibohm; Max Planck institutes, Oxford, Freiburg, Gothenburg) do not overlap with Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori, Ye or the B030 names. Statistical physics of turbulent particles and neural networks is distant from the fields of B018 and B041, which is a reason for me to defer on fine priority questions in both. I note Johansson's stated recusal on B020 and see no conflict of my own that requires recusal.
